# The book's data

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/setup.R")
```

Where do `gapminder_2007`, `medals` and `winds` come from, and how do you get
them?

[Data](data.qmd) was about a table of your own. This chapter is about the shared
tables that the book's examples draw from, listed in full under
[The tables](#the-tables). They are published
beside the book as CSV files, one per table, so you can run any example in this
book yourself. Each file has a fixed address:

```
https://psychometrician.github.io/gog-book/data/<name>.csv
```

`gapminder_2007.csv` holds the 142 countries drawn in the chapter
[A first plot](first-plot.qmd). `medals.csv` holds the medal counts drawn in
[Reading practice](reading.qmd), and `winds.csv` holds the wind observations
drawn in [Polar](polar.qmd).

Reading one takes a single call, `gog_table()`, which is part of the gog package
in all four languages. Nothing else needs to be installed.

`gog_table()` is a convenience: a quick way to read the book's tables from the
book's website. It is not a tool for reading or preparing data, and you do not
have to use it. A table you
read yourself, with readr in R, pandas in Python or any other reader you
already use, works the same in `data()`.
[Reading a table](#reading-a-table) says what to check when you do.

## Reading a table {#reading-a-table}

To run the first chapter's plot yourself, you need its table loaded in R,
Python, Julia or JavaScript. One line fetches it. `gog_table()` reads any of these tables by name:

```{r}
#| echo: false
peek(gapminder_2007)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
spellings(
  r = r"(gapminder_2007 <- gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life))",
  python = r"(gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life))",
  julia = r"(gapminder_2007 = gog_table("gapminder_2007")
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life))",
  js = r"(const gapminder_2007 = await gog_table("gapminder_2007");
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life));)"
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

*"Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life."*

Those four calls draw the same picture, because the table is the same file and
the engine is the same program.

A CSV file stores every value as text, so `gog_table()` converts each column
when it reads the file. A column becomes numbers when every value in it is a
number. An empty cell or `NA` counts as a missing value, not as text, so a
column of numbers with gaps still becomes numbers. Every other column stays text. This rule gives
the right type for most columns. It gives the wrong type for a label written as
a number, and for a date, which stays text. The `text` argument keeps a column as
text. Ten columns in these tables need it, and [Labels that
look like numbers](#labels-that-look-like-numbers), below, explains which and
why. `gog_table()` decides types this way so that the book's examples run with
nothing else installed. If you already use readr, pandas or another reader, set each
column's type there, where you can see and control it.

Why does a graphics package carry a table reader at all? R reads a CSV in one
call, and Python and Julia in a few lines. JavaScript has no CSV reader in its
standard library, and the work takes dozens of lines there, because a CSV
reader cannot simply split each line on commas. Six countries in `gapminder_2007.csv`
have a comma in the name, `"Congo, Dem. Rep."` among them, so that split gives
those rows seven fields, while the header has six. Nobody should have to paste
dozens of lines of parsing before drawing, so each package carries `gog_table()`
instead.

Each package fetches the file with what its language already has: R's
`read.csv()`, `urllib` in Python, `Downloads` in Julia and `fetch` in
JavaScript.

Read a file with a CSV reader of your own, and the rest of this chapter still
applies, because `data()` takes any table already in memory. You then do two
things yourself. First, check each column's type: your CSV reader decides it,
so the ten columns listed in [Labels that look like
numbers](#labels-that-look-like-numbers) need whatever that reader offers for
keeping a column as text. Second, declare the category order, because a CSV never records
one. You declare it with `factor()` in R, a pandas `Categorical` in Python, a
`CategoricalArray` in Julia, and `ordered()` in JavaScript. `gog_table()` does
not declare the order either, so after it, too, you declare the order yourself.
[Three things a CSV cannot record](#three-things-a-csv-cannot-record) covers
both, and dates as well.

Reading a different table is the same call with a different name:
`gog_table("winds")`, `gog_table("medals")`. `gog_table()` refuses a misspelled
name, and its message suggests the nearest published name, or points to the list under
[The tables](#the-tables).

## Three things a CSV cannot record {#three-things-a-csv-cannot-record}

A CSV records the values in a column, and never says what kind of column it is.
Three kinds of information are therefore lost when the file is written. You
restore them when you read the file. Each one changes the plot: the order of
the categories, whether an axis has one slot per value, and whether an axis is
a calendar. This chapter explains each one.

Restoring them is data preparation, and the tools you already use for your
data do it best: readr and `factor()` in R, pandas in Python, CSV.jl and
CategoricalArrays in Julia. This chapter shows how the book's own tables get
them only because `gog_table()` exists to read those tables quickly. For your
own data, do this work with those tools, before the table reaches `data()`.

### A declared order {#a-declared-order}

The eight compass points have a fixed order, and a plot of them reads correctly
only when its axis keeps that order. The `winds` table records one wind
observation per row:

```{r}
#| echo: false
winds <- read.csv("data/winds.csv")
peek(winds)
```

The `direction` column of `winds` holds the eight compass points. Their
order is N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW, clockwise from north. The
[Data](data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories) chapter shows how a declared
order sets the axis, the color assignment and the legend. A CSV cannot record
that declaration. `gog_table("winds")` therefore reads `direction` as plain
text, so you declare the order yourself after reading the file.

Until you declare an order, gog places the categories in the order they first
appear in the rows. The winds file lists its rows in compass order, so a plot
of `direction` made without the declaration reads correctly. Sort the rows by
`speed`, and the axis shows S, N, NE, NW, SE, E, SW, W. The plot still draws,
and nothing on it shows that the compass is in the wrong order.

The example below reads the table, sorts it by `speed` so that the rows are no
longer in compass order, and then declares the compass order:

```{r}
#| echo: false
spellings(
  r = r"(winds <- gog_table("winds")
# `base::order`, because gog's `order()` masks it
winds <- winds[base::order(winds$speed), ]
compass <- c("N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW")
winds$direction <- factor(winds$direction, levels = compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction))",
  python = r"(import pandas as pd

winds = gog_table("winds")
by_speed = sorted(enumerate(winds["speed"]), key=lambda pair: pair[1])
winds = {name: [column[i] for i, _ in by_speed]
         for name, column in winds.items()}
compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"]
winds["direction"] = pd.Categorical(winds["direction"], categories=compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(col.direction))",
  julia = r"(using CategoricalArrays

winds = gog_table("winds")
by_speed = sortperm(winds["speed"])
winds = Dict{String,Any}(name => column[by_speed] for (name, column) in winds)
compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"]
winds["direction"] = CategoricalArray(winds["direction"]; levels = compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(:direction))",
  js = r"(const winds = await gog_table("winds");
const by_speed = winds.speed.map((_, i) => i)
  .sort((a, b) => winds.speed[a] - winds.speed[b]);
for (const name in winds) winds[name] = by_speed.map((i) => winds[name][i]);
const compass = ["N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW"];
winds.direction = ordered(winds.direction, compass);

plot(data(winds), layer(bar, count), x(col.direction));)"
)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# The plot the four tabs above describe, drawn from the local copy of the same
# file, because the book does not fetch over the network while it builds.
winds <- read.csv("data/winds.csv")
winds <- winds[base::order(winds$speed), ]
compass <- c("N", "NE", "E", "SE", "S", "SW", "W", "NW")
winds$direction <- factor(winds$direction, levels = compass)

data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction)
```

*"Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction."*

The rows are in speed order, and the axis still reads N to NW. The declared
order decides the axis, not the order of the rows. A declared order is also kept
when the plot is drawn in another space, such as a circle. The [polar](polar.qmd) chapter draws these same counts of winds per direction as a
wind rose, and the change is one word. Add `polar()`, and the axis is drawn as a
circle, with N at the top and the rest clockwise from it:

```{r}
data(winds) + bar * count + x(direction) + polar()
```

*"Given the winds: bars derived by count, x is direction, in polar."*

The polar chapter explains that plot. The circle starts at the first
category and runs clockwise through the rest, so the compass reads correctly in
the flat plot and in the circle.

The example sorts the rows only to take them out of compass order, so that you
can see the declaration still works. The sort does not change the plot, so in
your own code you need only the declaration.

`direction` is one of many columns whose order the book declares. The list
below names every such column in the shared tables, with a short description of
each table. The last column says whether the file already lists the values in
the declared order.

| Table | What it holds | Column | Declared order | In order in the file? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `winds` | wind observations, one per row | `direction` | N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW | yes |
| | | `season` | Summer, Winter | no |
| `quakes_fiji` | 1,000 earthquakes near Fiji | `slab` | 0-90 km to 630-720 km, shallowest first | no |
| `six_weeks` | a shop's orders on 42 consecutive days | `weekday` | Mon to Sun | no |
| | | `week` | Week 1 to Week 6 | yes |
| `quakes_2011` | the earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more in 2011, week by week | `age` | this week, 1 week ago, 2 weeks ago, 3 weeks ago | yes |
| `cyclones` | the tracks of storms of hurricane strength, 1980 to 2025 | `month` | Jan to Dec | no |
| | | `category` | 1 or 2, 3 or 4, 5 | yes |
| `storm_seasons` | the same storms, counted by month, category and hemisphere | `month` | Jan to Dec | yes |
| | | `category` | 1 to 5 | yes |
| `census` | the population of two cities in each five-year age band | `age` | 0 to 85, youngest first | yes |
| `nightingale` | British army deaths in the Crimean War, by month and cause | `month` | Apr to Mar | yes |
| | | `cause` | Disease, Wounds, Other | yes |
| `titanic` | the people aboard the Titanic, in 32 groups | `class` | 1st, 2nd, 3rd, Crew | yes |
| | | `survived` | Yes, No | yes |
| `gm_twelve` | the life expectancy rank of twelve countries, 1952 to 2007 | `rank` | 1st to 12th | yes |
| `thermal_moments` | the flight of two gliders, sampled every two seconds | `moment` | 0 to 338 | yes |
| `listening` | weekly plays of four music genres over half a year | `genre` | Folk, Jazz, Techno, Ambient | yes |
| `cashflow` | the steps of a cash statement | `step` | Opening, Sales, Refunds, Costs, Tax, Closing | yes |
| `ripples` | wave heights in a shallow tank and a deep one | `tank` | Shallow, Deep | yes |
| `sessions` | 14 trading sessions, each with its open, close, high and low | `session` | 01 to 14 | yes |
| `sales_funnel` | the number of people at each stage of a sales funnel, in thousands | `stage` | Website visit, Downloads, Potential customers, Requested price, Invoice sent | yes |
| `cash_blocks` | `cashflow`, with the start and the end of each block of its waterfall | `step` | Opening, Sales, Refunds, Costs, Tax, Closing | yes |
| `candles` | `sessions` with the bottom and top of each candle's body | `session` | 01 to 14 | yes |
| `gm_eras` | the Gapminder countries in 1957 and 2007 | `era` | 1957, 2007 | yes |
| `gm_twelve_ends` | the same twelve countries as `gm_twelve`, in 1952 and 2007 | `year` | 1952, 2007 | yes |
| `gm_four` | the Gapminder countries in 1952, 1972, 1992 and 2007 | `period` | 1952, 1972, 1992, 2007 | yes |

A file that already lists its values in order still needs the declaration.
Without it, the plot keeps that order only until you sort the rows, as the example above
did. It is also lost when a sentence uses `order()`, which sorts undeclared
text alphabetically. (Given a column of numbers, `order()` sorts by size
instead; the labels in this list are text, so they are sorted alphabetically.) On the unsorted winds file, `order(direction)` puts the
compass points in the order E, N, NE, NW, S, SE, SW, W. For most columns in this
list, alphabetical order is also wrong: `10th` comes before `1st`, `10` comes before
`2`, and `Ambient` comes before `Folk`. The next section shows what happens to
`census` without its declaration.

### Labels that look like numbers {#labels-that-look-like-numbers}

The second thing a CSV cannot record is which columns are text. Ten columns
in these tables hold labels written as numbers, and `gog_table()` reads each of
them as numbers unless you name it in the `text` argument. Eight of their
tables are in the list above. The other two are new: `eras` holds the outline
of every country, with its life expectancy in 1957 and 2007. `ohio_turnout`
holds the share of each Ohio county's citizens who voted in three elections.
The list below names the ten columns.

| Table | Column | Example values | What the values name |
|---|---|---|---|
| `census` | `age` | `0`, `5`, `10`, ..., `85` | five-year age bands |
| `sessions` | `session` | `01`, `02`, ..., `14` | trading sessions |
| `candles` | `session` | `01`, `02`, ..., `14` | the same trading sessions, as in `sessions` |
| `gm_eras` | `era` | `1957`, `2007` | the two eras the rows compare |
| `gm_twelve_ends` | `year` | `1952`, `2007` | the two ends of a period |
| `ohio_turnout` | `election` | `2016`, `2020`, `2024` | three elections |
| `eras` | `era` | `1957`, `2007` | the two eras, as in `gm_eras` |
| `gm_four` | `period` | `1952`, `1972`, `1992`, `2007` | four years |
| `thermal_moments` | `moment` | `0`, `2`, `4`, ..., `338` | the samples of a flight |
| `storm_seasons` | `category` | `1` to `5` | the categories of a storm's strength |

Each of these values is a name, not a quantity. The `0` in `census` names the
youngest age band; it does not measure anything. `sessions` shows a second
problem: a number cannot keep a leading zero, so `gog_table()` reads `01` as
`1`. These two problems are the reason `gog_table()` takes a `text` argument:

```{r}
#| echo: false
spellings(
  r = r"(census <- gog_table("census", text = "age")
sessions <- gog_table("sessions", text = "session")
candles <- gog_table("candles", text = "session")
gm_eras <- gog_table("gm_eras", text = "era")
gm_twelve_ends <- gog_table("gm_twelve_ends", text = "year")
ohio_turnout <- gog_table("ohio_turnout", text = "election")
eras <- gog_table("eras", text = "era")
gm_four <- gog_table("gm_four", text = "period")
thermal_moments <- gog_table("thermal_moments", text = "moment")
storm_seasons <- gog_table("storm_seasons", text = "category"))",
  python = r"(census = gog_table("census", text=("age",))
sessions = gog_table("sessions", text=("session",))
candles = gog_table("candles", text=("session",))
gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text=("era",))
gm_twelve_ends = gog_table("gm_twelve_ends", text=("year",))
ohio_turnout = gog_table("ohio_turnout", text=("election",))
eras = gog_table("eras", text=("era",))
gm_four = gog_table("gm_four", text=("period",))
thermal_moments = gog_table("thermal_moments", text=("moment",))
storm_seasons = gog_table("storm_seasons", text=("category",)))",
  julia = r"(census = gog_table("census", text = ["age"])
sessions = gog_table("sessions", text = ["session"])
candles = gog_table("candles", text = ["session"])
gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text = ["era"])
gm_twelve_ends = gog_table("gm_twelve_ends", text = ["year"])
ohio_turnout = gog_table("ohio_turnout", text = ["election"])
eras = gog_table("eras", text = ["era"])
gm_four = gog_table("gm_four", text = ["period"])
thermal_moments = gog_table("thermal_moments", text = ["moment"])
storm_seasons = gog_table("storm_seasons", text = ["category"]))",
  js = r"(const census = await gog_table("census", ["age"]);
const sessions = await gog_table("sessions", ["session"]);
const candles = await gog_table("candles", ["session"]);
const gm_eras = await gog_table("gm_eras", ["era"]);
const gm_twelve_ends = await gog_table("gm_twelve_ends", ["year"]);
const ohio_turnout = await gog_table("ohio_turnout", ["election"]);
const eras = await gog_table("eras", ["era"]);
const gm_four = await gog_table("gm_four", ["period"]);
const thermal_moments = await gog_table("thermal_moments", ["moment"]);
const storm_seasons = await gog_table("storm_seasons", ["category"]);)"
)
```

Without the `text` argument, `age` becomes numbers. A `point` or a `line` then
places the bands along a continuous axis from 0 to 85, with ticks at 0, 20, 40,
60 and 80. No band gets its own slot. The plot still looks reasonable, so
nothing tells you the axis is wrong. With `age` read as numbers, the engine
also refuses the population pyramid's sentence in
[Many groups](cookbook/groups.qmd#where-does-a-population-pyramid-come-from),
because it sorts the bands with `order()`, and `order()` needs a
categorical axis. When `age` is read as text, it still needs its declared
order. Without the declaration, `order()` sorts the bands alphabetically, one
character at a time. The band 5 is then drawn between 45 and 50.

Each call above names one column, and a `text` argument can name more than
one. `gm_eras` holds the same values in two columns: `year` as a number, `era`
as a label. The calls above name only `era`, so `year` stays a number. To
read the year as a label too, name both columns in one `text` argument:

```{r}
#| echo: false
spellings(
  r = r"(gm_eras <- gog_table("gm_eras", text = c("year", "era")))",
  python = r"(gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text=("year", "era")))",
  julia = r"(gm_eras = gog_table("gm_eras", text = ["year", "era"]))",
  js = r"(const gm_eras = await gog_table("gm_eras", ["year", "era"]);)"
)
```

Each language writes more than one name in its own way. R puts them inside
`c()`, Python inside parentheses, and Julia and JavaScript inside square
brackets. In Python, one name can also be written alone, as in `text="age"`.
Inside parentheses it needs a trailing comma, as in `("age",)`, and two names do
not. In Julia and JavaScript, the second name is
added inside the brackets, after a comma.

Only `census`, `sessions`, `candles`, `gm_eras`, `gm_twelve_ends`, `ohio_turnout`,
`eras`, `gm_four`, `thermal_moments` and `storm_seasons` need a `text` argument; no other shared table
does.

### A date {#a-date}

The third thing a CSV cannot record is which columns are dates. Four tables
have a column of dates: `day` in `six_weeks` and in `revenue`, `at` in
`monitoring`, and `week` in `quakes_2011`. `gog_table()` returns each of them as
text, so the axis gets one slot per date instead of
a calendar axis. After reading, convert the column to your language's date or
timestamp type: in R, `as.Date()` for `six_weeks`, `revenue` and
`quakes_2011`, and `as.POSIXct()` for `monitoring`, which also records the hour.
In JavaScript, write a time after each date, so that it is midnight in local
time: `six_weeks.day.map((d) => new Date(d + "T00:00"))`. For `monitoring`,
which has a time already, replace the space with a `T`:
`new Date(t.replace(" ", "T"))`. The
[JavaScript](bindings/javascript.qmd#the-table-and-its-name) chapter explains
why.
[Scales](scales.qmd#time-a-date-column-gets-a-calendar-axis) shows the calendar
axis you get.

## The tables {#the-tables}

The list below names every table of the book, with its number of rows and
columns. The
[preface](index.qmd#the-cast) introduces the nine
families of table that most plots read. A family is one source split into
several tables, such as `gapminder_2007` and `gapminder_asia`, so the list is
longer than nine.

Tables outside those families are introduced in the chapter that first draws them.
Each name goes in place of `<name>` in the address at the top of this chapter. The
same name is what you give `gog_table()`:

```{r}
#| echo: false
files <- sort(list.files("data", pattern = "[.]csv$"))
info <- data.frame(
  Table = sub("[.]csv$", "", files),
  Rows  = vapply(files, function(f) nrow(read.csv(file.path("data", f))), integer(1)),
  Columns = vapply(files, function(f) ncol(read.csv(file.path("data", f))), integer(1))
)
knitr::kable(info, row.names = FALSE)
```

Some tables hold real data and some were made for this book. The tables whose names begin with
`gapminder` or `gm` hold figures from the Gapminder Foundation, which released
them into the public domain. So do `asia_2007`, `recent`, `three_continents` and `two_readings`.
`continents_2007`, `continent_means` and `world_median` are computed from those
figures.
`population_spikes`, `filled`, `eras` and `enclave` join them to
`world_borders`, the country outlines described below.
`iris_flowers`, `iris_measurements`, `petals`, `petal_stars`, `maunga_whau`, `peak`, `band`,
`relief`, `nyc_horizon`, `quakes_fiji` and `titanic` are reshaped from tables
included with R, and carry R's own license. `nightingale` is Florence Nightingale's table
of the British army's deaths in the Crimean War, 1854 to 1856. It comes from the
HistData package, under the same license as R's tables. `lung_survival` and
`lung_at_risk` come from R's `survival` package, under that package's own
license. `world_borders` is Natural Earth's
public-domain outline of the countries. `cyclones` and `storm_seasons` are US
government records: the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's
storms of hurricane strength, 1980 to 2025, as tracks and as counts. So are
`quakes_2011`, `us_counties` and `ohio_turnout`: the US Geological Survey's
earthquakes of magnitude 5 or more in 2011, the Census Bureau's counties of the
48 states between Canada and Mexico, with their
poverty rates in 2023, and the share of each Ohio county's citizens who voted
in 2016, 2020 and 2024, from the Election Assistance Commission and the Census
Bureau. Everything
else was made for this book, each table to show one thing; `census` is two plausible city profiles, not
a real census. The terms for each are in [`data/LICENSE.md`](data/LICENSE.md).

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A table holds the rows, and says nothing about how they look on the page.
[Choosing a mark](marks/index.qmd) shows how to pick the mark that draws them.
There are fourteen, and your question and your columns decide which one fits.
